children: Recent call for a three-day nationwide bank strike over the demand for a five-day work has moved the spotlight on the productivity of bank employees and extent of digitisation.

businessline analysis shows that the business growth generated by each employee of private sector banks has been higher at ₹19 crore per employee for the period between FY19 to FY26. This is slightly higher than the ₹17 crore business added by employees of public sector banks. Employees of foreign banks were, however, the most productive generating ₹43 crore per employee.

Productivity per employee is derived by dividing the addition to total credit and deposits by average number of employees in the two time periods – FY10 to FY18 and FY19 to FY26. Private sector banks witnessed a sharp increase in their business addition in the FY19 to FY26 period of 227 per cent, which was higher than the growth of 98 per cent recorded by PSBs.

But the difference in productivity is narrower because PSBs recorded a 5.6 per cent decline in employee count between FY19 and FY26, a drop of almost 45,000 employees. Meanwhile, employee count in private banks almost doubled, growing by 98 per cent between FY19 and FY26.

According to Vivek Iyer, Partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, “an extra day off is unlikely to move the business added or technology adoption numbers meaningfully. Where it can help is in retention, morale and fatigue. In thinly staffed branches, tired employees mean KYC lapses and operational errors, so this is as much a risk-management issue as a welfare one.”
Digitisation changes the case for physical presence

A recent Economic Advisory Council to the PM (EAC-PM) working paper measured the improvement in efficiency and productivity of Indian banking sector using data envelopment analysis (DEA), with technical efficiency capturing how effectively banks adopted technological innovations.

The authors’ calculated that the average technical-efficiency measure for PSBs rose from 81 per cent in FY19-FY22 to 92 per cent in FY23-FY26. Private banks, however, stood at 85 per cent of average technical efficiency in FY23-FY26, which according to the authors, “is primarily due to DCB Bank and IDFC First Bank. It seems takeover of weaker banks affected the efficiency in private sector.”
This adds another dimension to the five-day-week debate as by March 2026, 99.8 per cent of payments by volume and 97.85 per cent by value were conducted through digital channels.

“The real test is the customer. UPI, ATMs and continuous clearing have made Saturdays less critical for urban, digitally active customers, but not for cash-dependent traders, pensioners, daily-wage earners and rural households with limited business correspondent coverage,” explained Iyer.

A banking industry tracker, also talked about the impracticability of the five-day-week debate, by pointing out the difference between India and developed nations, where this is a practice. According to him, digital penetration is still not that high in India, with average daily footfalls close to 5 lakh in certain banks.

“If the joint IBA-UFBU committee builds in safeguards, such as rotational Saturday service at hub branches and stronger correspondent networks, five-day banking becomes a modernisation step aligned with practice at RBI, LIC and the markets. Without those safeguards, the burden shifts quietly onto the customers who can least absorb it. The decision should turn on access guarantees, not on productivity arguments from either side,” said Iyer.

title: Employees of private banks score over public sector banks in productivity
